Your perception surprises you

Bouba and kiki: sounds have shapes

Almost everyone calls a spiky shape "kiki" and a rounded one "bouba", whatever language they speak.

Imagine two shapes: one with sharp points, like a broken star, and one with soft curves, like a cloud. If you are told one is called kiki and the other bouba, which is which? Almost everyone gives the same answer: the spiky one is kiki and the rounded one bouba.

From Köhler to Ramachandran

Wolfgang Köhler described the phenomenon in 1929 with the made-up words takete and maluma. In 2001, V. S. Ramachandran and Edward Hubbard repeated it with bouba and kiki, and more than 90% of people agreed. A 2022 study with speakers of 25 languages, using different writing systems, found the effect in most of them.

It is thought that the shape of the mouth when pronouncing, rounded for "bouba" and tense for "kiki", and the sharpness of the consonants link sound and shape. It suggests that the relationship between words and their meanings is not always entirely arbitrary, and it might have helped language to arise.

References

  1. Ramachandran, V. S. y Hubbard, E. M. (2001). Synaesthesia: a window into perception, thought and language. Journal of Consciousness Studies, 8(12), 3–34.
  2. Ćwiek, A. et al. (2022). The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 377(1841), 20200390.
